Probably yes, but only if closing costs are reasonable. The 0.6-point spread is modest, so the decision hinges on what the refi costs you.

Over 10 years, 5.9% vs. 6.5% on $400k saves about $24k gross: roughly $155/month lower payment (~$18.6k) plus ~$5.4k more principal paid down. Subtract closing costs, typically 2–5% of the loan ($8k–$20k):

| Closing costs | Net 10-yr gain | Breakeven |
|---|---|---|
| $6k | ~$18k | ~3 yrs |
| $10k | ~$14k | ~4–5 yrs |
| $16k | ~$8k | ~7 yrs |
| $20k+ | marginal | ~8+ yrs |

These figures assume a 30-year loan in both cases. A few things change the math:

- **Term reset.** If your current loan has, say, 25 years left and you take a new 30-year, the lower monthly payment overstates the savings because you're stretching repayment. Compare like terms (refi into a 25-year, or keep paying your old amount) or you'll pay more total interest.
- **Points.** If 5.9% requires buying points, those are closing costs and lengthen breakeven. Get a no-points quote to compare.
- **Rates falling further.** If rates drop more, refinancing twice means paying closing costs twice. A no-cost or low-cost refi (slightly higher rate, lender covers fees) can keep that option open.
- **Your stay is uncertain.** "About 10 years" gives margin at low costs. At high costs, moving at year 6 could leave you roughly break-even.

Get a Loan Estimate and check total lender plus third-party fees. If they're under about $10k, refinance. If they're near $20k, it's not worth the hassle and risk.
